examples.en: I'm a Christian, so I go to church every Sunday.

examples.ko: 기독교인의 가정에서 자라서 성경 이야기를 많이 들었어요.
examples.en: I grew up in a Christian family, so I heard a lot of Bible stories.
He is a Christian, but he respects other religions too.
My mother is a devout Christian.
There are many Christian students at this school.

examples.ko: 제 친구는 기독교인이 된 지 오 년이 됐어요.
examples.en: It has been five years since my friend became a Christian.

explain: '크리스천'이라고도 많이 말하고, '기독교 신자'나 '신자'도 비슷하게 써요. 한국에서 '기독교'는 흔히 개신교를 가리킬 때가 많아서, 천주교는 '천주교 신자'나 '가톨릭 신자'라고 따로 말하는 경우가 많아요.
explain_en: People also say '크리스천', and '기독교 신자' or '신자' are used in a similar way. In Korea '기독교' often refers to Protestantism, so Catholics are often called '천주교 신자' or '가톨릭 신자' separately.

examples.en: This summer a record-breaking heat wave went on and on.
The water pipes froze because of the record-breaking cold wave.
They say this month's sales are at a record level.
Yesterday it snowed a record amount.
That movie had a record-breaking box office run.

examples.ko: 내일 기록적인 추위가 온다고 해서 두꺼운 옷을 샀어요.
examples.en: They said record-breaking cold is coming tomorrow, so I bought thick clothes.

explain: 보통 '기록적인'이나 '기록적으로'로 쓰고, 날씨나 숫자를 전하는 뉴스에서 특히 많이 나와요. 사람의 개인 기록보다는 '이례적으로 대단한 수준'이라는 느낌으로 말해요.
explain_en: It is usually used as '기록적인' or '기록적으로', and appears especially often in news about weather and numbers. It gives the feeling of an unusually extreme level rather than a person's personal record.

examples.en: A lot of grease has built up on the kitchen hood.

examples.ko: 세제로 닦아도 기름때가 잘 안 지워져요.
examples.en: Even when I scrub with detergent, the grease stains don't come off easily.
I used baking soda to get rid of the grease on the gas stove.
The work clothes are covered with oil stains.

examples.ko: 손에 묻은 기름때는 비누로 씻으면 돼요.
examples.en: You can wash the grease off your hands with soap.

examples.ko: 오래된 기름때에는 뜨거운 물이 효과가 있어요.
examples.en: Hot water works on old, built-up grease.

explain: 주방이나 자동차, 기계처럼 기름이 닿는 곳에 쓰는 말이에요. '기름때가 끼다', '기름때가 묻다', '기름때를 닦다'처럼 짝지어 써요.
explain_en: It is used for places touched by oil, such as kitchens, cars and machines. It pairs with verbs like '기름때가 끼다' (build up), '기름때가 묻다' (get stained) and '기름때를 닦다' (wipe off).

examples.en: An oil slick has spread over the sea, and the fishermen are worried.

examples.ko: 사고로 생긴 기름띠를 제거하는 작업이 한창이에요.
examples.en: Work to remove the oil slick caused by the accident is in full swing.
An oil slick is floating around on the water.
The beach closed because of the oil slick.
The oil slick was pushed to the shore by the wind.
They rescued a seagull covered in an oil slick.

explain: 주로 배 사고 같은 뉴스에서 바다나 강 위에 기름이 띠처럼 퍼진 모습을 말할 때 써요. 일상에서는 '기름이 떠 있다'처럼 풀어서 말할 때가 많아요.
explain_en: It is mostly used in news, such as about ship accidents, for oil spread in a band over the sea or a river. In everyday talk people often just say '기름이 떠 있다' (oil is floating).

examples.en: My face was shiny, so I blotted it with oil-blotting paper.

examples.ko: 여름에는 가방에 기름종이를 꼭 넣고 다녀요.
examples.en: In summer I always carry oil-blotting paper in my bag.

examples.ko: 기름종이 한 장이면 코 기름이 싹 없어져요.
examples.en: One sheet of blotting paper wipes away the oil on your nose.

examples.ko: 기름종이가 다 떨어져서 사러 가야 해요.
examples.en: I've run out of blotting paper, so I have to go buy some.
They sell oil-blotting paper at convenience stores too.
My friend gave me blotting paper as a birthday present.

explain: 주로 얼굴의 기름기를 닦는 얇은 종이를 말해요. 요리할 때 튀김 기름을 빼는 종이는 보통 '키친타월'이라고 해요.
explain_en: It mostly means thin paper for blotting oil off your face. The paper used to soak up oil from fried food is usually called '키친타월' (kitchen towel).

examples.en: The door creaked, so I oiled the hinges.

examples.ko: 자전거 체인에 기름칠을 하면 훨씬 부드러워요.
examples.en: If you oil the bicycle chain, it runs much more smoothly.
After I oiled it, the door became quiet.

examples.ko: 기계는 가끔 기름칠을 해 줘야 오래 써요.
examples.en: You have to oil machines now and then to use them for a long time.
Maybe it needs more oil, because the wheel is making noise.
My father oils his tools every month.

explain: 보통 '기름칠을 하다'나 '기름칠하다'로 써요. 기계나 문이 부드럽게 움직이도록 기름을 바르는 것이고, 비유로도 쓰여요.

phrases.example: 일이 잘 풀리도록 담당자에게 미리 기름칠해 뒀어요.
phrases.en: I greased the person in charge beforehand so things would go smoothly.
phrases.nuance_ko: 윗사람이나 담당자에게 선물이나 돈으로 잘 보이려 할 때 쓰는 비유예요. 약간 부정적이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: A figurative use for winning over a superior or official with gifts or money. It sounds slightly negative.

explain_en: It is usually used as '기름칠을 하다' or '기름칠하다'. It literally means putting oil on machines or doors so they move smoothly, and it is also used figuratively.

en: person who acts on their mood

examples.ko: 제 남자친구는 기분파라서 갑자기 여행을 가자고 해요.
examples.en: My boyfriend goes by his mood, so he suddenly suggests going on a trip.

examples.ko: 기분파인 언니는 기분이 좋으면 밥을 크게 사요.
examples.en: My sister goes by her mood, and when she's in a good mood she treats everyone to a big meal.

examples.ko: 저는 기분파가 아니라서 계획 없이 움직이는 게 불편해요.
examples.en: I'm not a go-by-my-mood person, so moving without a plan is uncomfortable.

examples.ko: 기분파 상사 때문에 눈치를 많이 봐요.
examples.en: I have to read the room a lot because of my moody boss.
That friend totally acts on their mood.
Mood-driven people also change their minds quickly.

explain: 그날그날의 기분에 따라 행동하거나 결정하는 사람을 가볍게 부르는 말이에요. 기분이 좋을 때 돈을 잘 쓰는 사람에게도 쓰고, 상황에 따라 칭찬이 될 수도 놀림이 될 수도 있어요.
explain_en: It is a casual word for someone who acts or decides according to their mood of the day. It is also used for people who spend generously when they feel good, and depending on the situation it can be a compliment or a tease.

en: publish; print; write an article about something

examples.en: That incident hasn't been turned into a news article yet.
The reporter wrote up the tip as an article.
I asked them to run the company's news as an article.
I heard the newspaper decided to publish this story.

examples.ko: 연예인의 사생활을 함부로 기사화하면 안 돼요.
examples.en: You shouldn't carelessly turn a celebrity's private life into an article.

examples.ko: 인터뷰 내용을 기사화하려면 본인 허락이 필요해요.
examples.en: To publish the interview as an article, you need the person's permission.

explain: '기사로 쓰다'나 '기사로 내다'와 같은 뜻이고, 뉴스나 신문 이야기에서 자주 나와요. 같은 내용을 '기사화되다'로 말하면 기사로 나오게 된다는 뜻이 돼요.
explain_en: It is the same idea as '기사로 쓰다' or '기사로 내다' and often appears in talk about news and newspapers. The passive form '기사화되다' means that something gets published as an article.

examples.en: Ready-made clothes are cheaper than tailored ones.

examples.ko: 저는 키가 작아서 기성복을 사면 늘 줄여야 해요.
examples.en: I'm short, so whenever I buy ready-made clothes I always have to have them shortened.
These days even ready-made clothes come in a variety of designs.

examples.ko: 기성복 매장에서 정장을 한 벌 샀어요.
examples.en: I bought a suit at a ready-to-wear shop.

examples.ko: 기성복이 몸에 안 맞아서 맞춤 양복을 맞췄어요.
examples.en: Ready-made clothes didn't fit me, so I had a suit made to measure.

examples.ko: 어렸을 때는 기성복보다 어머니가 만든 옷을 많이 입었어요.
examples.en: When I was little, I wore clothes my mother made more than store-bought ones.

explain: 반대말은 '맞춤복'이나 '맞춤옷'이에요. 일상에서는 '사 입는 옷'이라고도 하고, '기성'은 '기성세대'처럼 이미 만들어져 있다는 뜻으로도 나와요.
explain_en: Its opposite is '맞춤복' or '맞춤옷' (made-to-measure clothes). In everyday talk people also say '사 입는 옷' (clothes you buy), and '기성' also appears in words like '기성세대' (the established generation) with the sense of 'already made or established'.

examples.en: Our company's technical team solved the problem.
We posted a notice to hire a new technical team.
It was easy to understand after hearing the technical team's explanation.
The broadcast technical crew checked the equipment all night.
The technical team and the designers had a meeting together.
An overseas technical team is also taking part in this project.

explain: '-진'은 어떤 일을 하는 사람들의 팀을 가리켜요. '의료진', '연구진', '제작진'처럼 뉴스에서 많이 보여요. 한 사람은 '기술자'라고 해요.
explain_en: '-진' refers to a team of people doing a certain kind of work, as in '의료진' (medical staff), '연구진' (research team) and '제작진' (production crew), which are common in the news. A single person is called '기술자'.

examples.en: The tiled roofs of hanok houses are beautiful.

examples.ko: 비 오는 날 기와지붕을 보면 운치가 있어요.
examples.en: A tiled roof on a rainy day has a lovely atmosphere.
My grandfather's house has a tiled roof.
A cat is sitting on the tiled roof.
Snow has piled up softly on the tiled roof.
The cafe with a tiled roof is popular.

explain: 흙으로 구워 만든 '기와'를 얹은 지붕이에요. 한옥이나 궁, 절 이야기에서 자주 나오고, 풀이나 볏짚으로 만든 '초가지붕'과 짝으로 말하곤 해요.
explain_en: It is a roof covered with '기와', tiles made of baked clay. It often comes up when talking about hanok, palaces and temples, and is often paired with '초가지붕', a roof made of straw.

examples.en: Since we're already here, let's look around before we go.
Now that you've started, try to see it through.

examples.ko: 기왕에 살 거면 좋은 걸로 사요.
examples.en: If you're going to buy it anyway, buy a good one.

examples.ko: 기왕에 하는 김에 청소도 해 주세요.
examples.en: While you're at it, please do the cleaning too.

examples.ko: 기왕에 이렇게 된 거 맛있는 거나 먹으러 가요.
examples.en: Since it turned out this way, let's go eat something tasty.
If you're going anyway, leave early.

explain: 이미 그렇게 된 상황이니 이왕 하는 김에 더 좋게 하자는 말투로 자주 써요. '이왕에'라고도 하고, 뒤에 '-(으)니', '-는 김에', '-(으)ㄹ 거면'이 많이 따라와요.
explain_en: It is often used to say that since things are already this way, you might as well do it better. People also say '이왕에', and it is commonly followed by '-(으)니', '-는 김에' or '-(으)ㄹ 거면'.

examples.en: He miraculously survived the accident.
It was a miraculous recovery that even the doctors found astonishing.
That team pulled off a miraculous comeback win.
Miraculously, I arrived in time for the exam.
I prayed for a miracle to happen.
It's miraculous that nobody was hurt.

explain: '기적적인 회복', '기적적으로 살아남다'처럼 '기적적인'이나 '기적적으로' 형태로 가장 많이 써요. 말 그대로 기적 같을 때뿐 아니라 '운이 정말 좋았다'는 느낌으로 가볍게도 말해요.
explain_en: It is most often used as '기적적인' or '기적적으로', as in '기적적인 회복' (a miraculous recovery) or '기적적으로 살아남다' (to survive miraculously). It is used not only for true miracles but also lightly, to say that someone was really lucky.

en: be discouraged; be downhearted; be downcast

examples.ko: 시험을 망쳐서 하루 종일 기죽어 있었어요.
examples.en: I bombed the exam and was downhearted all day.
I got scolded in front of my friends and lost my confidence.

examples.ko: 너무 기죽지 말고 다음에 잘하면 돼요.
examples.en: Don't be too discouraged, just do well next time.

examples.ko: 아이가 기죽을까 봐 칭찬을 많이 해 줬어요.
examples.en: I praised the child a lot so that he wouldn't lose heart.
She answered in a dispirited voice.

examples.ko: 비싼 가게에 들어가면 괜히 기죽게 돼요.
examples.en: When I walk into an expensive shop, I somehow feel intimidated.

explain: '기(氣)가 죽다'가 줄어든 모양이고 '기가 죽다'로 띄어 쓰는 말도 흔해요. 자신감이나 활기가 없어질 때 쓰고, 반대는 '기(가) 살다'예요.
explain_en: It is a contracted form of '기(氣)가 죽다', and the spaced form '기가 죽다' is also common. It is used when someone loses confidence or energy, and the opposite is '기(가) 살다'.

examples.ko: 상대 팀 응원 소리가 우리를 기죽였어요.
examples.en: The other team's cheering intimidated us.
Don't discourage the child, encourage him.

examples.ko: 일부러 후배를 기죽이려고 한 말은 아니에요.
examples.en: I didn't say it on purpose to dishearten my junior.

examples.ko: 그 선수는 큰 덩치로 상대를 기죽여요.
examples.en: That player intimidates opponents with his big build.
Don't say things that bring your friend down.

examples.ko: 비싼 가방 자랑으로 사람들을 기죽이고 싶지 않아요.
examples.en: I don't want to make people feel small by showing off an expensive bag.

explain: '기죽다'의 사동 표현이라서 '누가 누구를 기죽이다' 모양으로 써요. '기를 죽이다'로도 말하고, 반대는 '기를 살려 주다'예요.
explain_en: It is the causative form of '기죽다', so it is used in the pattern 'someone discourages someone'. It can also be said as '기를 죽이다', and the opposite is '기를 살려 주다' (to boost someone's spirits).

examples.ko: 집 앞에 기찻길이 있어서 기차 소리가 들려요.
examples.en: There is a railroad in front of my house, so I can hear the trains.
When I was little, I walked along the railroad.
The railroad is dangerous, so you must not cross it.
A train passes slowly over the tracks.
The old railroad has been turned into a walking path.
I stopped for a moment at the railroad crossing.

explain: '철길'과 같은 뜻으로 쓰는 말이에요. '철도'는 열차 교통 전체를 말할 때가 많고, '기찻길'은 열차가 다니는 길 그 자체를 말할 때 써요.
explain_en: It means the same as '철길'. '철도' often refers to the whole railway system, while '기찻길' refers to the path the train runs on.

examples.ko: 기초적인 한국어 질문은 할 수 있어요.
examples.en: I can ask basic questions in Korean.
This is a really elementary mistake.
I'll start by explaining what you need to know at the basic level.
I'm studying again from the basic concepts of math.
That much is basic, so everyone knows it.
Please show me the basic way to use a computer.

explain: '기본적'과 비슷하지만 '기초적'은 처음 배우는 쉬운 단계라는 느낌이 더 커요. '기본적'은 중요하고 바탕이 되는 것이라는 느낌으로 많이 써요.
explain_en: It is similar to '기본적', but '기초적' has more of a feeling of an easy first stage that you learn at the beginning. '기본적' is often used for something important that forms the foundation.

examples.ko: 기초화장을 먼저 하고 색조 화장을 해요.
examples.en: I do my skincare base first and then color makeup.
I only do the basic skincare step before going out.
Your makeup won't flake if your base skincare goes on well.
My skin is dry, so I pay attention to my base skincare.

examples.ko: 기초화장은 보통 스킨, 로션 순서로 해요.
examples.en: For basic skincare you usually go in the order of toner then lotion.
I bought new basic skincare products.

explain: 스킨, 로션, 크림처럼 피부를 정리하는 단계를 말해요. 색을 입히는 '색조 화장'과 짝으로 말하고, 보통 기초화장을 먼저 해요.
explain_en: It refers to the skin-prep step with toner, lotion and cream. It is paired with '색조 화장' (color makeup), and you usually do the base skincare first.

examples.en: An accident happened, so an emergency meeting was held.
The team leader suddenly called an emergency meeting.
I couldn't eat lunch because of the emergency meeting.
I was late for my appointment because I attended an emergency meeting.
The emergency meeting ended in an hour.
Today's schedule all changed because of the emergency meeting.

explain: 갑자기 생긴 급한 일 때문에 여는 회의예요. '긴급회의를 열다', '긴급회의를 소집하다'처럼 쓰고, 회사와 뉴스에서 많이 나와요.
explain_en: It is a meeting held because of a sudden urgent matter. It is used as '긴급회의를 열다' or '긴급회의를 소집하다' and appears often at work and in the news.

examples.en: The police were dispatched urgently after receiving the report.
Something urgent came up that I needed to contact you about, so I called.
This document has to be handled urgently.
They rushed the patient to the hospital.

examples.ko: 긴급히 필요한 물건이 있으면 말씀해 주세요.
examples.en: If there's anything you urgently need, please tell me.
The company is urgently looking for someone.

explain: '급히'와 비슷한데 '긴급히'가 더 격식 있고 뉴스나 공지에서 자주 나와요. 일상 대화에서는 '급하게'를 더 많이 말해요.
explain_en: It is similar to '급히', but '긴급히' is more formal and appears often in news and announcements. In everyday conversation people use '급하게' more.

examples.ko: 새 신발이 발에 길들 때까지 조금 아파요.
examples.en: The new shoes hurt a little until they get broken in.

examples.ko: 이 강아지는 아직 사람에게 길들지 않았어요.
examples.en: This puppy hasn't become used to people yet.
New sneakers get comfortable once they're broken in.

examples.ko: 손에 길든 도구가 제일 쓰기 편해요.
examples.en: Tools that your hands are used to are the easiest to use.

examples.ko: 고양이가 집에 길드는 데 시간이 걸렸어요.
examples.en: It took time for the cat to get used to the house.
Children quickly get used to a new environment.

explain: 동물이 사람에게 익숙해지거나 물건이 쓰면서 부드러워질 때 써요. 누가 길들이는 것은 '길들이다'이고, '길들여지다'도 비슷하게 쓰여요. 어간의 ㄹ이 빠져서 '길드는', '길든'이 돼요.
explain_en: It is used when an animal gets used to people or an item becomes softer through use. When someone does the taming it is '길들이다', and '길들여지다' is used in a similar way. The ㄹ of the stem drops, giving forms like '길드는' and '길든'.

examples.en: The cola has gone flat, so it doesn't taste good.
I don't want to drink flat soda.
I left the lid open and it went flat.
The story ended in an anticlimax and I was disappointed.
I sang a song so that the mood wouldn't go flat.

examples.ko: 김빠질까 봐 탄산음료는 뚜껑을 꼭 닫아요.
examples.en: I close fizzy drinks tightly so they don't go flat.

explain: '김이 빠지다'가 줄어든 말이고, 탄산음료의 기포가 없어질 때와 재미나 흥이 없어질 때 모두 써요. 비슷한 '김새다'는 기대나 흥이 갑자기 꺾일 때 더 자주 말해요.
explain_en: It is a contracted form of '김이 빠지다' and is used both when a fizzy drink loses its bubbles and when the fun or excitement fades. The similar '김새다' is used more often when expectations or excitement suddenly get deflated.

examples.en: I prepared everything and now it's canceled, what a letdown.
You told me the ending first, so it ruined the fun.
Why spoil it by telling me in advance?

examples.ko: 기대했던 경기가 일찍 끝나서 김샌 기분이에요.
examples.en: The game I was looking forward to ended early, so I feel let down.

examples.ko: 이제 와서 안 가겠다고 하면 김새잖아요.
examples.en: If you say you won't go now, it kills the mood.

examples.ko: 김새지 않게 계획은 비밀로 해 주세요.
examples.en: Please keep the plan secret so it doesn't spoil the fun.

explain: '김이 새다'가 줄어든 구어체 표현이고, 기대하거나 신나던 마음이 갑자기 꺾일 때 써요. 친한 사이에서 편하게 하는 말이라 윗사람에게는 조심해서 써요.
explain_en: It is a contracted spoken form of '김이 새다' and is used when excitement or anticipation suddenly gets deflated. It is casual talk between close people, so be careful using it with superiors.

examples.en: When kimchi-making season comes, the price of napa cabbage goes up.
My family gathers every kimchi-making season.
The market is really crowded during kimchi-making season.

examples.ko: 김장철을 맞아 마트에서 소금 할인을 해요.
examples.en: For kimchi-making season, the supermarket is discounting salt.
I ordered chili powder to get ready for kimchi-making season.
This year even during kimchi-making season, the weather is warm.

explain: 겨울을 대비해 김치를 많이 담그는 늦가을 무렵을 말해요. '철'은 '휴가철', '장마철'처럼 어떤 일이 많은 시기를 뜻하고, 짝말로 '김장하다', '김장 김치'가 있어요.
explain_en: It refers to the late-autumn period when people make a lot of kimchi to prepare for winter. '철' means a season when something is common, as in '휴가철' and '장마철', and related words are '김장하다' and '김장 김치'.

examples.ko: 까놓고 말하면 저는 그 계획이 별로예요.
examples.en: To be frank, I'm not a fan of that plan.
I feel relieved now that I've opened up about how I really feel.

examples.ko: 우리 사이에 까놓지 못할 말이 뭐가 있어요?
examples.en: Is there anything we can't say frankly between us?
Now is the time to put everything on the table.
That friend has the type of personality to say everything openly.
After I laid it all out, I actually felt refreshed.

explain: 주로 '까놓고 말하면', '까놓고 이야기하다'처럼 써요. 숨기거나 돌려 말하지 않고 있는 그대로 말하는 구어 표현이에요. '털어놓다'는 비밀이나 고민을 말할 때 많이 쓰고, '까놓다'는 격의 없이 솔직하게 말한다는 느낌이 있어요.
explain_en: It is mostly used as '까놓고 말하면' or '까놓고 이야기하다'. It is a spoken expression for saying things as they are, without hiding or beating around the bush. '털어놓다' is often used for confessing secrets or worries, while '까놓다' feels more like speaking frankly and openly.

examples.ko: 비행기에서 내려다보니 땅이 까마득히 멀어 보였어요.
examples.en: Looking down from the plane, the ground looked incredibly far away.
I looked up at the dizzyingly tall building.

examples.ko: 어릴 적 일이라 까마득히 잊고 있었어요.
examples.en: It happened in my childhood, so I had completely forgotten it.

examples.ko: 그때 일은 까마득히 먼 옛날 이야기 같아요.
examples.en: That time feels like a story from the distant past.
The summit is still a long, long way off.
I totally forgot about the appointment.

explain: '아득히'와 비슷하게 거리나 높이가 매우 멀 때 쓰고, 시간이나 기억에도 써요. '까마득히 잊다'처럼 완전히 잊었다는 뜻으로도 자주 말해요.
explain_en: Like '아득히', it is used when distance or height is very great, and it also applies to time and memory. It is often used in '까마득히 잊다' to mean having forgotten something completely.

examples.en: I played all summer, so my face became tanned.
My younger sibling has dark skin and looks healthy.
Her white teeth look pretty against her dark skin.
My arms are dark from being in the sun.
Her skin is dark, but her face is clear and pretty.
Children with deeply tanned skin are playing on the beach.

explain: 주로 사람의 피부가 약간 검은 모습을 말해요. '가무잡잡하다'와 비슷한 말이고, '거무스름하다'보다 피부에 쓸 때가 더 많아요. 칭찬이 될 때도 있지만 상대에 따라 조심해서 써요.
explain_en: It mainly describes skin that is somewhat dark. It is similar to '가무잡잡하다', and compared with '거무스름하다' it is more often used for skin. It can sound like a compliment, but use it carefully depending on the person.

examples.en: Oh well, let's just give it a try.
If I fail, big deal, I'll just take it again.

examples.ko: 까짓것 못 할 게 뭐 있어요?
examples.en: What's to stop us? We can do it.
No big deal, I can just earn the money again.
Who cares, let's eat as much as we want today!
It's no big deal if you get it wrong.

explain: 어려움이나 손해를 대수롭지 않게 여기고 '그래, 해 보자' 하며 마음먹을 때 문장 앞에 붙여요. 걱정을 털어내는 결심의 느낌이 있어서, 남의 일에 관심이 없다는 뜻의 'who cares'와는 조금 달라요. 구어에서는 '까짓거'로도 자주 말해요. 허물없는 말투라서 윗사람에게는 쓰지 않는 게 좋아요.
explain_en: You put it at the start of a sentence when you decide to shrug off a difficulty or loss and say, 'Fine, let's do it.' It carries a sense of resolve, so it differs a little from 'who cares', which suggests indifference. In speech it is often said as '까짓거'. It is casual, so avoid it with superiors.

examples.ko: 키가 작아서 까치발을 하고 선반에 손을 뻗었어요.
examples.en: I'm short, so I stood on tiptoe and reached for the shelf.
I walked on tiptoe so the baby wouldn't wake up.

examples.ko: 까치발을 들면 공연이 좀 더 잘 보여요.
examples.en: If you stand on tiptoe, you can see the performance a little better.
The tiptoe-raise exercise is good for your calves.
Standing on tiptoe was hard, so I came down quickly.
My calves hurt from standing on tiptoe.

explain: 발뒤꿈치를 들고 발끝으로 서는 자세예요. '까치발을 하다', '까치발을 들다', '까치발로 걷다'처럼 써요. 건물에서 선반을 받치는 부품도 '까치발'이라고 해요.
explain_en: It is the posture of lifting your heels and standing on your toes. It is used as '까치발을 하다', '까치발을 들다' or '까치발로 걷다'. The bracket that supports a shelf is also called '까치발'.

examples.ko: 그 친구는 깍쟁이라서 밥값을 한 번도 안 내요.
examples.en: That friend is stingy and never pays for a meal.
Have you heard the expression 'Seoul smart-aleck'?
My younger sibling is a little skinflint who won't lend toys.

examples.ko: 깍쟁이처럼 굴지 말고 좀 나눠 먹어요.
examples.en: Don't be so selfish, share some of it.

examples.ko: 그렇게 깍쟁이 같은 소리 하지 마요.
examples.en: Don't say such selfish things.

examples.ko: 깍쟁이 같지만 알고 보면 정이 많아요.
examples.en: She seems calculating, but she's actually warm-hearted.

explain: 자기 것만 챙기고 남에게 잘 베풀지 않는 사람, 또는 약삭빠르고 얄미운 사람을 말해요. 아이나 친한 사이에서는 가볍게 놀리는 말로도 쓰지만, 어른에게 하면 기분 나빠할 수 있어요.

phrases.en: They say Seoul people are shrewd, and you really are quick with numbers.
phrases.nuance_ko: 서울 사람은 약삭빠르고 인색하다는 옛 선입견을 담은 표현이에요. 지금은 농담처럼 쓰는 편이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: An expression reflecting an old stereotype that Seoul people are shrewd and stingy. Today it is mostly used jokingly.

explain_en: It refers to a person who looks after only their own interests and doesn't give to others, or someone shrewd and a bit annoying. It is also used as a light tease with children or close friends, but it can offend if said to an adult.

examples.ko: 남을 깎아내려서 자기가 높아지는 건 아니에요.
examples.en: Putting others down doesn't make you any higher.
He tends to belittle his colleagues' achievements.
Please don't belittle my efforts.

examples.ko: 경쟁 상대를 깎아내리는 광고는 좋지 않아요.
examples.en: Ads that run down the competition are not good.
I didn't say it on purpose to put you down.

examples.ko: 사람들이 그 작품을 깎아내렸지만 저는 좋아요.
examples.en: People disparaged the work, but I like it.

explain: 다른 사람이나 그의 가치, 평판을 실제보다 낮게 말할 때 써요. 반대는 '치켜세우다'나 '띄워 주다'예요. '헐뜯다'는 더 직접적으로 흉을 보는 느낌이에요.
explain_en: It is used when you speak of a person, or their value or reputation, as lower than it really is. The opposites are '치켜세우다' and '띄워 주다'. '헐뜯다' feels more like directly badmouthing someone.

en: Chinese-style fried chicken in spicy sweet sauce

examples.en: We ordered kkanpunggi at the Chinese restaurant.
Kkanpunggi is sweet and a little spicy.
Kkanpunggi and jajangmyeon, please.
We shared one order of kkanpunggi.
The kkanpunggi is crispy and delicious.
I found a great kkanpunggi place with delicious sauce.

explain: 한국식 중국집에서 먹는 닭튀김 요리예요. 탕수육처럼 튀긴 요리지만 소스가 달라서 보통 매콤달콤한 맛이 나요.
explain_en: It is a fried chicken dish eaten at Korean-style Chinese restaurants. It is fried like 탕수육, but the sauce is different, so it usually tastes sweet and spicy.

examples.en: I spread a mat on the floor and sat down.
The mat is thin, so the floor feels cold.

examples.ko: 강아지 집에 부드러운 깔개를 넣어 줬어요.
examples.en: I put a soft pad in the dog's house.
I did yoga on this mat.

examples.ko: 이 깔개는 세탁기로 빨 수 있어요.
examples.en: You can wash this mat in the washing machine.
I bought a new cushion pad for the chair.

explain: 바닥이나 의자 위에 까는 물건을 두루 가리키는 말이에요. 방석, 돗자리, 매트는 각각 이름이 따로 있고, '깔개'는 그 모두를 넓게 부를 때 쓸 수 있어요.
explain_en: It is a broad word for things laid on a floor or on a chair. Cushions, picnic mats and exercise mats each have their own names, and '깔개' can be used to refer to all of them in general.

examples.en: The children are running around laughing out loud.
My friend's story was funny, so I burst out laughing.

examples.ko: 방 안에서 깔깔 웃는 소리가 들려요.
examples.en: I can hear giggling coming from the room.

examples.ko: 둘이 깔깔 웃느라 수업에 집중을 못 했어요.
examples.en: The two of us were giggling and couldn't focus on class.
My younger sibling ran away laughing.
I burst into laughter while watching the video.

explain: 주로 '깔깔 웃다'로 쓰고, 소리가 크고 밝게 터지는 웃음을 말해요. 억누르듯 장난스럽게 웃는 '낄낄'과는 느낌이 달라요.
explain_en: It is mostly used as '깔깔 웃다' and describes laughter that bursts out loudly and brightly. It feels different from '낄낄', which is a stifled, mischievous kind of laugh.

examples.en: The kids are giggling while watching a cartoon.

examples.ko: 친구들과 깔깔거리다 보니 시간이 훌쩍 갔어요.
examples.en: While laughing with my friends, the time just flew by.
The sound of loud laughter woke me up.
You must not guffaw in the library.
My sister burst out laughing even at trivial things.
Don't just stand there laughing, help me a bit.

explain: '깔깔'에 '-거리다'가 붙어 소리 내어 웃는 행동이 계속된다는 뜻이에요. '깔깔대다'와 거의 같은 뜻이라서 바꿔 써도 돼요.
explain_en: '-거리다' is added to '깔깔' to show that the loud laughing keeps going. It means almost the same as '깔깔대다', so the two can be swapped.

examples.en: The students are laughing loudly during break time.
The teacher came because my friends were laughing so loudly.
We chatted and laughed our heads off all night.
The child giggled because of the tickling.
Stop cackling and be quiet.
The room that had been full of laughter suddenly went quiet.

explain: '깔깔'에 '-대다'가 붙은 말로, 소리 내어 크게 웃는 행동이 이어진다는 뜻이에요. '깔깔거리다'와 거의 같은 뜻이라서 바꿔 써도 돼요.
explain_en: '-대다' is added to '깔깔' to show that the loud laughing continues. It means almost the same as '깔깔거리다', so the two can be swapped.
